question: A pathology slide shows eosinophilic, glassy membranes lining alveoli after acute lung injury. Which diagnosis best fits this histologic finding?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Diffuse alveolar damage consistent with ARDS
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are the acute lesion of DAD/ARDS; they are fibrin-rich eosinophilic membranes lining alveoli, matching the slide.

options.text: Usual interstitial pneumonia pattern of fibrosis
options.rationale: UIP shows patchy subpleural fibrosis and fibroblastic foci rather than acute hyaline membranes; if chronic patchwork fibrosis were present it could be UIP.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with loose granulomas
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis features lymphocytic inflammation and loosely formed granulomas, not hyaline membranes; granulomas on biopsy would support that diagnosis.

options.text: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with proteinaceous material
options.rationale: Alveolar proteinosis has intra-alveolar surfactant-like proteinaceous material but lacks classic hyaline membranes lining alveoli; bronchoalveolar lavage with PAS-positive material would support it.

options.text: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia with macrophage filling
options.rationale: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia shows abundant intra-alveolar macrophages, not hyaline membranes; a macrophage-rich picture would make this correct.

question: Which drug from the mnemonic 'BBC MAN' is correctly paired with causing pulmonary interstitial fibrosis?
cited_learning_objective: List drugs known to cause (as a side effect) pulmonary (interstitial) fibrosis.

options.text: Bleomycin is associated with pulmonary fibrosis
options.rationale: Bleomycin is listed among drugs (B in BBC MAN) that can cause pulmonary fibrosis; its pulmonary toxicity is a classic cause of interstitial fibrosis.

options.text: Metformin commonly causes interstitial lung fibrosis
options.rationale: Metformin is not in the lecture list; if a drug were listed in BBC MAN (e.g., methotrexate) it would be correct instead.

options.text: Nitrofurantoin never causes pulmonary fibrosis
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin (N in BBC MAN) can cause pulmonary fibrosis; stating it never does contradicts the lecture and would be correct only if removed from the list.

options.text: Amoxicillin is a frequent cause of fibrosis
options.rationale: Amoxicillin is not in the lecture mnemonic; a drug from BBC MAN such as amiodarone would be the correct antibiotic-related example if present.

options.text: Cyclophosphamide is unrelated to lung fibrosis
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide (C in BBC MAN) is listed as causing pulmonary fibrosis; saying it is unrelated contradicts the lecture and would be correct only if omitted from the mnemonic.

question: Which radiographic pattern is most characteristic of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis on HRCT?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Reticulation with subpleural honeycombing predominance
options.rationale: IPF/UIP shows reticulation with honeycombing and subpleural, lower-lobe predominance on HRCT, matching this option.

options.text: Upper lobe nodular cavitary lesions with consolidation
options.rationale: Upper lobe cavitary nodules suggest infections or granulomatous disease, not UIP; if HRCT showed upper lobe cavitation this option would be correct.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar airspace consolidation without fibrosis
options.rationale: Diffuse airspace consolidation without fibrosis is more typical of acute alveolar processes like pneumonia or ARDS, not chronic UIP.

options.text: Bilateral perihilar ground glass with cardiomegaly
options.rationale: Perihilar ground glass with cardiomegaly suggests cardiogenic pulmonary edema; absence of subpleural reticulation would make UIP unlikely.

options.text: Miliary nodules diffusely scattered throughout lungs
options.rationale: Miliary nodules suggest hematogenous infection or metastases, not the subpleural reticulation and honeycombing of UIP.

question: Which histologic feature defines the chronic, organizing phase after severe alveolar injury?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Interstitial and intra-alveolar fibroblastic proliferation
options.rationale: The proliferative/organizing phase of DAD features fibroblastic proliferation in interstitium and alveoli leading to fibrosis, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Tight noncaseating granulomas in alveolar walls
options.rationale: Tight noncaseating granulomas are characteristic of sarcoidosis, not the organizing phase of DAD; granulomas on biopsy would support sarcoidosis instead.

options.text: Abundant intra-alveolar macrophages with pigment
options.rationale: Intra-alveolar macrophages with anthracotic pigment suggest smoking or anthracosis, not fibroblastic proliferation of organizing DAD.

options.text: Extensive eosinophilic proteinaceous alveolar casts
options.rationale: Proteinaceous casts are seen in alveolar proteinosis or acute edema; organizing DAD is defined by fibroblasts and collagen deposition.

options.text: Necrotizing vasculitis with cavitating nodules
options.rationale: Necrotizing vasculitis with cavitation is typical of GPA/Wegener, not the fibroblastic organizing phase of DAD.

question: A miner with progressive dyspnea has upper-lobe fibrotic nodules with birefringent particles on polarized light. Which occupational disease is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Silicosis from crystalline silica exposure
options.rationale: Silicosis features fibrotic silicotic nodules and birefringent silica particles under polarized light, matching the lecture description.

options.text: Coal workers pneumoconiosis from coal dust
options.rationale: CWP shows anthracotic pigment and coal macules; birefringent silica particles are not typical unless silica contaminant is present.

options.text: Asbestosis with lower lobe subpleural fibrosis
options.rationale: Asbestosis preferentially affects lower lobes and shows ferruginous bodies, not birefringent silica particles in upper-lobe nodules.

options.text: Berylliosis causing noncaseating granulomas
options.rationale: Berylliosis produces nonnecrotizing granulomas resembling sarcoidosis, not silicotic nodules with birefringent particles.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with loose granulomas
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis shows lymphocytic inflammation and loose granulomas, not silica-associated birefringent nodules.

question: Which pleural finding is most specifically associated with asbestos exposure on gross exam?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Pleural plaques on parietal pleura surfaces
options.rationale: Pleural plaques are characteristic of asbestos exposure and often localize to the parietal pleura, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Upper lobe progressive massive fibrosis nodules
options.rationale: Progressive massive fibrosis is seen in complicated CWP, not specifically with asbestos; upper-lobe PMF would support CWP instead.

options.text: Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes
options.rationale: Eggshell calcification is classically associated with silicosis, not asbestos; finding eggshell calcification would favor silicosis.

options.text: Diffuse miliary nodules throughout lung parenchyma
options.rationale: Miliary nodules suggest hematogenous infection or metastases, not asbestos-related pleural plaques; miliary pattern would change the diagnosis.

options.text: Tight noncaseating granulomas in lung parenchyma
options.rationale: Tight noncaseating granulomas are typical of sarcoidosis or berylliosis, not asbestos exposure; granulomas would suggest those etiologies.

question: A patient with chronic dyspnea has subpleural fibrosis and patchy 'patchwork' interstitial scarring with fibroblastic foci on biopsy. Which histopathologic pattern is this?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Usual interstitial pneumonia pattern consistent with IPF
options.rationale: UIP is defined by subpleural fibrosis, patchy interstitial fibrosis with a patchwork pattern and fibroblastic foci, matching the biopsy.

options.text: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia with uniform fibrosis
options.rationale: NSIP shows more temporally uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis, not the temporal heterogeneity and fibroblastic foci of UIP.

options.text: Organizing pneumonia with intra-alveolar plugs
options.rationale: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia features polypoid plugs of organizing connective tissue in alveoli and bronchioles, not patchy subpleural fibrosis.

options.text: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia with macrophages
options.rationale: DIP shows abundant intra-alveolar macrophages and more uniform involvement, not the patchy subpleural fibrosis and fibroblastic foci of UIP.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with loose granulomas
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis has lymphocytic inflammation and loosely formed granulomas, not the patchwork fibrosis and fibroblastic foci of UIP.

question: Which laboratory or diagnostic test would be most useful to exclude infectious causes before diagnosing sarcoidosis?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify sarcoidosis.

options.text: Tuberculosis testing such as PPD or IGRA assay
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion; TB testing helps exclude mycobacterial infection which can produce granulomas similar to sarcoidosis.

options.text: Serum antinuclear antibody testing for autoimmune disease
options.rationale: ANA may help evaluate connective tissue disease but does not exclude infectious granulomatous causes; a positive ANA would suggest autoimmune overlap.

options.text: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level for emphysema risk
options.rationale: Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing assesses emphysema risk and is unrelated to excluding infectious granulomatous disease; it would not clarify granuloma etiology.

options.text: Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension
options.rationale: Echocardiography evaluates cardiac consequences like pulmonary hypertension but does not exclude infectious causes of granulomas; it would be supportive, not exclusionary.

options.text: Serum cryptococcal antigen for fungal infection
options.rationale: Cryptococcal antigen can detect cryptococcosis but is not the primary test to exclude TB; targeted microbiologic studies including TB testing are more central before diagnosing sarcoidosis.

question: Which pathologic description best matches hypersensitivity pneumonitis on lung biopsy?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Patchy peribronchiolar chronic inflammation with loose granulomas
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis shows patchy peri-bronchiolar chronic inflammation with loosely formed granulomas, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Tight well-formed noncaseating granulomas throughout lung
options.rationale: Tight well-formed granulomas are characteristic of sarcoidosis; if granulomas were tight and widespread, sarcoidosis would be favored.

options.text: Diffuse hyaline membranes lining alveoli in acute injury
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are seen in DAD/ARDS acute lesions, not the chronic lymphocytic inflammation and loose granulomas of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

options.text: Ferruginous bodies with subpleural fibrosis and plaques
options.rationale: Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies and pleural plaques indicate asbestos exposure, not hypersensitivity pneumonitis; their presence would suggest asbestosis.

options.text: Numerous intra-alveolar macrophages with anthracotic pigment
options.rationale: Anthracotic pigment and macrophages suggest coal dust exposure or urban pollution, not the immune-mediated granulomatous inflammation of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

question: A patient with acute respiratory failure has bilateral patchy alveolar opacities on chest x-ray without cardiomegaly. Which syndrome does this radiograph most suggest?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Acute respiratory distress syndrome causing diffuse opacities
options.rationale: ARDS typically shows bilateral patchy alveolar opacities without cardiomegaly on chest x-ray, consistent with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and DAD.

options.text: Left ventricular failure with cardiogenic pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema usually shows cardiomegaly and vascular congestion; absence of cardiomegaly makes LV failure less likely.

options.text: Lobar bacterial pneumonia with air bronchograms
options.rationale: Lobar pneumonia often produces focal consolidation rather than diffuse bilateral patchy opacities; focal lobar findings would support pneumonia.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism causing wedge-shaped infarcts
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism typically causes peripheral wedge-shaped infarcts or normal radiographs; diffuse bilateral opacities without cardiomegaly are not classic for PE.

options.text: Chronic interstitial fibrosis with honeycombing
options.rationale: Chronic fibrosis shows reticulation and honeycombing rather than acute bilateral patchy alveolar opacities; chronic imaging features would differ.

question: Which occupational exposure is most associated with increased susceptibility to tuberculosis according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Silica exposure leading to silicosis increases TB risk
options.rationale: Silicosis impairs macrophage function and is associated with increased susceptibility to tuberculosis, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Coal dust exposure in CWP directly increases TB risk
options.rationale: CWP involves anthracosis and fibrosis but the lecture specifically highlights silica as increasing TB susceptibility; coal dust alone is less strongly linked.

options.text: Asbestos exposure is the primary TB risk factor
options.rationale: Asbestos exposure is linked to mesothelioma and lung cancer, not specifically increased TB susceptibility; finding ferruginous bodies would suggest asbestos.

options.text: Beryllium exposure commonly causes TB reactivation
options.rationale: Beryllium causes granulomatous disease resembling sarcoidosis but is not described as increasing TB risk; positive TB testing would be needed to implicate TB.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis exposure increases TB risk
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is immune-mediated to organic antigens and is not associated with increased TB susceptibility; microbiologic evidence would be required.

question: Which histologic feature differentiates sarcoidosis from hypersensitivity pneumonitis on lung biopsy?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Tight well-formed noncaseating granulomas in sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis is characterized by tight, well-formed noncaseating granulomas, whereas hypersensitivity pneumonitis has loosely formed granulomas and more bronchiolocentric inflammation.

options.text: Loose poorly formed granulomas in sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Loose granulomas are typical of hypersensitivity pneumonitis; if granulomas were loose and peri-bronchiolar, HP would be favored.

options.text: Hyaline membranes lining alveoli in sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are features of DAD/ARDS, not sarcoidosis; their presence would suggest acute lung injury instead.

options.text: Ferruginous bodies within macrophages in sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies indicate asbestos exposure, not sarcoidosis; finding iron-coated fibers would change the diagnosis to asbestosis.

options.text: Birefringent silica particles in sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Birefringent silica particles are seen in silicosis; their presence would favor silica-related disease rather than sarcoidosis.

question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis and multiple well-defined pulmonary nodules after years of mining exposure most likely has which syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Caplan syndrome (rheumatoid pneumoconiosis) is most likely
options.rationale: Caplan syndrome is the combination of RA and pneumoconiosis with multiple pulmonary nodules in patients with dust exposure, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Usual interstitial pneumonia unrelated to RA exposure
options.rationale: UIP/IPF is idiopathic and not specifically linked to RA plus dust exposure; presence of RA and nodules favors Caplan syndrome.

options.text: Silicosis without any relation to rheumatoid arthritis
options.rationale: Silicosis causes fibrotic nodules but the combination with RA and multiple well-defined nodules is characteristic of Caplan syndrome rather than isolated silicosis.

options.text: Sarcoidosis causing rheumatoid-like joint disease
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis can cause systemic findings but the specific association of RA with pneumoconiosis nodules defines Caplan syndrome; sarcoidosis would require noncaseating granulomas without RA history.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from organic antigens
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is immune-mediated to organic antigens and typically presents with diffuse interstitial changes and loose granulomas, not RA-associated nodules from mining dust.

question: Which microscopic finding is most characteristic of silicosis nodules?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Central whorled collagen with peripheral dust-laden macrophages
options.rationale: Silicotic nodules classically have a central whorled collagen core with peripheral dust-laden macrophages, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Ferruginous bodies coated with iron and protein
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies are associated with asbestos exposure; their presence would favor asbestosis rather than silicosis.

options.text: Numerous intra-alveolar macrophages with anthracotic pigment
options.rationale: Anthracotic pigment and macrophages suggest coal dust exposure (CWP), not the whorled collagen nodules of silicosis.

options.text: Tight noncaseating granulomas with asteroid bodies
options.rationale: Tight granulomas with asteroid bodies are seen in sarcoidosis, not silicotic nodules; granulomas would change the differential.

options.text: Hyaline membranes lining alveoli in acute injury
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are features of DAD/ARDS and not characteristic of silicosis; their presence would indicate acute lung injury.

question: A patient with progressive dyspnea has cobblestoned pleural surfaces and lower-lobe predominant fibrosis grossly. Which exposure or disease does this most suggest?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with subpleural scarring
options.rationale: IPF/UIP causes cobblestoned pleural surfaces from subpleural retraction and lower-lobe predominant fibrosis, matching the gross description.

options.text: Silicosis causing upper-lobe fibrotic nodules
options.rationale: Silicosis typically affects upper lobes with silicotic nodules; lower-lobe cobblestoning would not fit silicosis unless disease distribution were atypical.

options.text: Asbestosis with pleural plaques and lower-lobe fibrosis
options.rationale: Asbestosis can cause lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques; however, cobblestoned pleural retraction and UIP pattern favor IPF unless asbestos bodies are identified.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with bronchiolocentric fibrosis
options.rationale: HP often shows peri-bronchiolar fibrosis and loose granulomas; gross cobblestoning and subpleural honeycombing are more typical of UIP.

options.text: Coal workers pneumoconiosis with progressive massive fibrosis
options.rationale: CWP PMF usually affects upper lobes and forms large fibrotic scars; lower-lobe cobblestoning would be atypical for PMF.

question: A 45-year-old bird breeder develops fever, cough, and dyspnea 6 hours after exposure. Imaging shows bilateral interstitial nodular pattern. Which mechanism best explains her disease?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Immune complex and T cell mediated reaction to inhaled antigen
options.rationale: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis involves a mixed type III and IV hypersensitivity to inhaled organic antigens, producing interstitial inflammation and granulomas.

options.text: Direct cytotoxicity of inhaled particles causing necrosis
options.rationale: Direct cytotoxicity causing necrosis is not the primary mechanism in HP; if biopsy showed widespread necrosis without granulomas, direct toxicity might be considered.

options.text: IgE mediated bronchospasm without interstitial inflammation
options.rationale: IgE-mediated allergic asthma causes bronchospasm and eosinophilia, not the interstitial lymphocytic inflammation and granulomas of HP; elevated IgE and reversible airflow obstruction would support asthma.

options.text: Macrophage ingestion of inorganic fibers causing fibrosis
options.rationale: Macrophage ingestion of inorganic fibers describes pneumoconioses like asbestosis or silicosis, not the immune-mediated HP; finding ferruginous bodies or birefringent particles would support pneumoconiosis.

options.text: Autoimmune vasculitis causing necrotizing granulomas
options.rationale: Necrotizing vasculitis with granulomas suggests GPA/Wegener, which presents with renal involvement and c-ANCA positivity, not the exposure-related HP described.

question: A 60-year-old man with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure has heavy, wet lungs at autopsy and hyaline membranes microscopically. Which pathophysiologic process most directly produced the hyaline membranes?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Alveolar epithelial and endothelial injury with protein-rich edema
options.rationale: DAD/ARDS involves epithelial and endothelial cell death with increased vascular permeability and leakage of protein-rich fluid that forms hyaline membranes.

options.text: Chronic fibroblast proliferation producing collagen scar
options.rationale: Chronic fibroblast proliferation leads to fibrosis in organizing DAD or UIP, not the acute hyaline membrane formation from proteinaceous edema.

options.text: Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia producing surfactant excess
options.rationale: Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia occurs during repair but does not create hyaline membranes; if surfactant dysfunction predominated, neonatal hyaline membrane disease would be considered.

options.text: Immune granulomatous inflammation with giant cells
options.rationale: Granulomatous inflammation produces granulomas and giant cells, not hyaline membranes; granulomas on biopsy would indicate sarcoidosis or HP.

options.text: Iron-coated fibers inducing localized pleural plaques
options.rationale: Iron-coated (ferruginous) bodies and pleural plaques are features of asbestos exposure, unrelated to acute hyaline membrane formation in ARDS.

question: Which diagnostic stain would best highlight iron-coated asbestos bodies in lung tissue?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Prussian blue stain to detect iron in ferruginous bodies
options.rationale: Prussian blue highlights iron and is used to demonstrate ferruginous (asbestos) bodies coated with iron-protein complexes, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli detection
options.rationale: Ziehl-Neelsen detects mycobacteria (acid-fast bacilli), not iron-coated fibers; positive AFB staining would indicate mycobacterial infection.

options.text: Mucicarmine stain for mucinous capsule detection
options.rationale: Mucicarmine highlights cryptococcal capsule mucin, not iron in asbestos bodies; a mucicarmine-positive yeast would suggest cryptococcosis.

options.text: Masson trichrome stain for collagen fibrosis assessment
options.rationale: Masson trichrome highlights collagen and is useful for fibrosis assessment, but it does not specifically detect iron-coated asbestos bodies; Prussian blue would be needed for iron.

options.text: Periodic acid Schiff stain for polysaccharide detection
options.rationale: PAS stains glycogen and fungal cell walls, not iron-coated fibers; PAS positivity would suggest fungal elements or mucopolysaccharides.

question: A 59-year-old professor with 3 years of progressive dyspnea has HRCT showing subpleural lower-lobe reticulation and biopsy with patchy interstitial fibrosis. Which two diagnoses best correspond to clinician and pathologist perspectives?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Clinician: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; pathologist: UIP
options.rationale: Clinically the syndrome is IPF and histopathologically the pattern is UIP; the lecture explicitly distinguishes clinician (IPF) and pathologist (UIP) terminology.

options.text: Clinician: silicosis; pathologist: silicotic nodules
options.rationale: Silicosis would require occupational silica exposure and birefringent particles; absence of exposure and subpleural UIP features make silicosis unlikely.

options.text: Clinician: sarcoidosis; pathologist: noncaseating granulomas
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis shows tight noncaseating granulomas and often hilar adenopathy; biopsy showing patchy fibrosis and fibroblastic foci supports UIP/IPF instead.

options.text: Clinician: hypersensitivity pneumonitis; pathologist: loose granulomas
options.rationale: HP would show peri-bronchiolar inflammation and loose granulomas; the described subpleural reticulation and patchy fibrosis favor UIP/IPF.

options.text: Clinician: asbestosis; pathologist: ferruginous bodies present
options.rationale: Asbestosis would be supported by asbestos exposure and ferruginous bodies; absence of asbestos bodies or exposure makes this pairing incorrect.

question: Which clinical feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of ARDS rather than cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Bilateral alveolar infiltrates without cardiomegaly on chest x-ray
options.rationale: ARDS typically presents with bilateral patchy alveolar infiltrates and absence of cardiomegaly, distinguishing it from cardiogenic pulmonary edema which usually shows cardiomegaly.

options.text: Elevated brain natriuretic peptide indicating heart failure
options.rationale: Elevated BNP suggests cardiogenic edema from heart failure; a low BNP would be more consistent with ARDS in the appropriate clinical context.

options.text: Rapid improvement with diuretics and afterload reduction
options.rationale: Improvement with diuretics supports cardiogenic pulmonary edema; lack of response to diuretics would favor ARDS.

options.text: Presence of ferruginous bodies on sputum cytology
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies indicate asbestos exposure and are unrelated to distinguishing ARDS from cardiogenic edema; their presence would suggest asbestos-related disease.

options.text: Upper-lobe predominant nodular fibrosis on imaging
options.rationale: Upper-lobe nodular fibrosis suggests pneumoconiosis like silicosis or CWP, not the acute bilateral alveolar process of ARDS.

question: A worker exposed to beryllium develops nonnecrotizing granulomas in the lung. Which diagnosis and mechanism best fit this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Chronic berylliosis due to cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity
options.rationale: Berylliosis is a type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity causing nonnecrotizing granulomas that can mimic sarcoidosis, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Silicosis from silica causing caseating granulomas
options.rationale: Silicosis produces silicotic nodules and fibrosis, not nonnecrotizing granulomas; caseating granulomas would suggest TB rather than silicosis.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from bird antigen causing tight granulomas
options.rationale: HP causes loosely formed granulomas and peri-bronchiolar inflammation; tight granulomas are more typical of sarcoidosis or berylliosis.

options.text: Asbestosis producing ferruginous bodies and granulomas
options.rationale: Asbestosis is associated with ferruginous bodies and fibrosis, not nonnecrotizing granulomas; finding iron-coated fibers would support asbestosis.

options.text: Wegener granulomatosis causing necrotizing granulomas
options.rationale: GPA/Wegener causes necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis with renal involvement and c-ANCA positivity, differing from nonnecrotizing beryllium granulomas.

question: Which feature on lung biopsy would most strongly favor a diagnosis of UIP over nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Temporal heterogeneity with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing
options.rationale: UIP shows temporal heterogeneity with early fibroblastic foci alongside established fibrosis and honeycomb change, distinguishing it from the temporally uniform NSIP.

options.text: Temporally uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis
options.rationale: Temporally uniform fibrosis is characteristic of NSIP; finding uniformity would favor NSIP over UIP.

options.text: Loose peri-bronchiolar granulomas and lymphocytes
options.rationale: Loose granulomas and bronchiolocentric inflammation suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not UIP; their presence would change the diagnosis.

options.text: Abundant intra-alveolar macrophages with pigment
options.rationale: Intra-alveolar macrophages with anthracotic pigment suggest smoking-related disease or anthracosis, not UIP; such macrophage predominance would point elsewhere.

options.text: Necrotizing vasculitis with crescentic glomerulonephritis
options.rationale: Necrotizing vasculitis and renal crescents indicate GPA/Wegener, not UIP; systemic vasculitis findings would redirect the diagnosis.

question: A patient with ARDS who survives the acute phase later develops progressive interstitial fibrosis. Which minority outcome described in the lecture does this represent?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Progression from DAD to chronic interstitial fibrosis
options.rationale: A minority of ARDS patients progress from acute DAD to chronic interstitial fibrosis and scarring, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Immediate resolution without any residual scarring
options.rationale: Many patients recover without fibrosis, but the question asks about the minority outcome of progression to fibrosis; immediate resolution would not match the described minority outcome.

options.text: Development of ferruginous bodies and mesothelioma
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies and mesothelioma are asbestos-related and unrelated to post-ARDS fibrosis; their presence would indicate asbestos exposure.

options.text: Transformation into desquamative interstitial pneumonia pattern
options.rationale: DIP is smoking-related with macrophage accumulation and is not the typical chronic outcome of ARDS; finding macrophage-predominant DIP would suggest a different etiology.

options.text: Conversion to granulomatous disease like sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause and is not a typical sequela of ARDS; granulomas on biopsy would indicate sarcoidosis or other granulomatous disease.

question: Which clinical test would you order to evaluate a suspected case of Wegener granulomatosis presenting with sinusitis, lung mass, and hematuria?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify sarcoidosis.

options.text: c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) serology to support GPA diagnosis
options.rationale: GPA/Wegener is strongly associated with c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA positivity, which is a key diagnostic marker mentioned in the lecture.

options.text: Serum angiotensin converting enzyme for sarcoidosis
options.rationale: ACE levels can be elevated in sarcoidosis but are not diagnostic for GPA; a positive c-ANCA would be more specific for GPA.

options.text: Prussian blue stain to detect iron-coated fibers
options.rationale: Prussian blue detects iron in ferruginous bodies from asbestos exposure, not vasculitis; its positivity would suggest asbestos-related disease.

options.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli in sputum
options.rationale: Ziehl-Neelsen identifies mycobacterial infection; while TB can mimic granulomatous disease, c-ANCA testing is the targeted test for GPA in this clinical scenario.

options.text: Serum cryptococcal antigen for fungal infection
options.rationale: Cryptococcal antigen detects cryptococcosis and is not the primary test for GPA; fungal testing would be considered if infectious causes were suspected.

question: Which gross lung appearance corresponds to advanced honeycomb change described in end-stage interstitial lung disease?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Cystic spaces lined by bronchiolar epithelium (honeycombing)
options.rationale: Honeycomb lung consists of cystic spaces lined by bronchiolar or respiratory epithelium resulting from dense fibrosis and architectural destruction, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Red, heavy, wet lungs without architectural distortion
options.rationale: Red, heavy, wet lungs describe acute DAD/ARDS grossly, not chronic honeycomb change; chronic architectural distortion would be absent in this description.

options.text: Multiple small granulomas with central caseation
options.rationale: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis or certain fungal infections, not honeycomb fibrosis; presence of caseation would change the diagnosis.

options.text: Numerous ferruginous bodies on pleural surface
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies indicate asbestos exposure and may accompany fibrosis, but they do not describe the cystic honeycomb architecture of end-stage interstitial lung disease.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar macrophage accumulation with pigment
options.rationale: Macrophage accumulation with anthracotic pigment suggests anthracosis or smoking-related disease, not the cystic honeycomb change of end-stage fibrosis.

question: A patient with chronic cough has tight, well-formed noncaseating granulomas and bilateral hilar adenopathy. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify sarcoidosis.

options.text: Sarcoidosis presenting with noncaseating granulomas and adenopathy
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis is characterized by tight, well-formed noncaseating granulomas and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, matching the clinical and pathologic findings.

options.text: Tuberculosis with caseating granulomas and cavitation
options.rationale: TB typically produces caseating granulomas and may cavitate; noncaseating granulomas and bilateral hilar adenopathy favor sarcoidosis over TB.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with loose granulomas and fever
options.rationale: HP shows loosely formed granulomas and peri-bronchiolar inflammation often with fever after exposure; tight granulomas and prominent hilar adenopathy point toward sarcoidosis.

options.text: Silicosis with silicotic nodules and eggshell calcification
options.rationale: Silicosis produces silicotic nodules and may show eggshell calcification of nodes, but the granulomas are not typically tight noncaseating granulomas as in sarcoidosis.

options.text: Wegener granulomatosis with necrotizing granulomas and hematuria
options.rationale: GPA causes necrotizing granulomas and renal involvement; nonnecrotizing tight granulomas with isolated hilar adenopathy are more consistent with sarcoidosis.

question: Which occupational particle size range is most dangerous because it reaches small airways and settles in their linings?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Particles 1 to 5 micrometers in diameter are most dangerous
options.rationale: The lecture states particles 1–5 μm in diameter are most dangerous because they can reach small airways and deposit in their linings.

options.text: Particles larger than 10 micrometers are most dangerous
options.rationale: Larger particles (>10 μm) are usually trapped in upper airways and less likely to reach small airways; smaller 1–5 μm particles are the primary concern.

options.text: Nanoparticles under 0.1 micrometers are most dangerous
options.rationale: While nanoparticles can have unique effects, the lecture specifically highlights 1–5 μm particles as most dangerous for deposition in small airways.

options.text: Particles exactly 0.5 micrometers are most dangerous
options.rationale: The lecture gives a range (1–5 μm); a single value of 0.5 μm falls outside that range and would not match the stated most dangerous size.

options.text: Particles between 6 and 10 micrometers are most dangerous
options.rationale: Particles 6–10 μm are less likely to reach the small airways compared with the 1–5 μm range emphasized in the lecture.

question: Which finding on polarized light microscopy supports a diagnosis of silicosis?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Birefringent silica particles visible under polarized light
options.rationale: Silica particles are birefringent under polarized light and their presence supports silicosis, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Iron-coated ferruginous bodies staining with Prussian blue
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies indicate asbestos exposure and stain for iron; their presence would favor asbestosis rather than silicosis.

options.text: Numerous anthracotic pigment-laden macrophages
options.rationale: Anthracotic pigment-laden macrophages suggest coal dust exposure (CWP), not the birefringent silica particles of silicosis.

options.text: Tight noncaseating granulomas with asteroid bodies
options.rationale: Tight granulomas with asteroid bodies are seen in sarcoidosis, not silicosis; granulomas would shift the differential diagnosis.

options.text: Hyaline membranes lining alveoli in acute injury
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are features of DAD/ARDS and are unrelated to the polarized-light birefringence seen in silicosis.

question: A patient with chronic interstitial lung disease has HRCT showing lower-lobe predominant reticulation and honeycombing. Which management consideration follows from the lecture's prognosis for this condition?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Poor response to steroids and median survival three to five years
options.rationale: IPF/UIP typically responds poorly to steroids and has an average survival of 3–5 years after diagnosis, as stated in the lecture.

options.text: Excellent steroid responsiveness and full recovery expected
options.rationale: IPF generally responds poorly to steroids; excellent steroid responsiveness would contradict the lecture and suggest a different diagnosis like NSIP.

options.text: Immediate improvement with antifungal therapy is expected
options.rationale: Antifungal therapy is not a standard treatment for IPF; improvement with antifungals would indicate an infectious etiology rather than IPF.

options.text: Spontaneous resolution without progressive fibrosis is typical
options.rationale: IPF is progressive with poor prognosis; spontaneous resolution would be atypical and suggest an alternative reversible process.

options.text: Lung transplantation is contraindicated in all cases
options.rationale: Lung transplantation may be considered for advanced IPF; stating it is universally contraindicated contradicts management options discussed for end-stage disease.

question: Which histologic lesion is the acute hallmark of diffuse alveolar damage seen in ARDS?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Hyaline membranes lining alveolar walls are the acute hallmark
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes composed of fibrin-rich edema fluid and necrotic cell remnants are the acute lesion of DAD/ARDS, per the lecture.

options.text: Tight noncaseating granulomas are the acute hallmark
options.rationale: Tight noncaseating granulomas are characteristic of sarcoidosis, not the acute lesion of DAD/ARDS; their presence would indicate granulomatous disease.

options.text: Ferruginous bodies are the acute hallmark
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies indicate asbestos exposure and are not the acute lesion of DAD; their presence would suggest asbestosis.

options.text: Whorled collagen nodules are the acute hallmark
options.rationale: Whorled collagen nodules describe silicotic nodules in silicosis, not the hyaline membranes of acute DAD.

options.text: Loose granulomas with lymphocytes are the acute hallmark
options.rationale: Loose granulomas with lymphocytes suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not the hyaline membranes of acute DAD/ARDS.

question: Which clinical history element would most strongly suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis rather than sarcoidosis in a patient with interstitial lung disease?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Recurrent symptoms hours after exposure to bird proteins
options.rationale: HP is triggered by inhaled organic antigens with symptoms appearing hours after exposure and recurring with re-exposure, distinguishing it from sarcoidosis.

options.text: Young adult with bilateral hilar adenopathy and skin lesions
options.rationale: Bilateral hilar adenopathy and systemic findings are classic for sarcoidosis; absence of exposure history would favor sarcoidosis.

options.text: Long history of asbestos insulation work with plaques
options.rationale: Asbestos exposure with pleural plaques suggests asbestosis, not HP; occupational exposure to organic antigens is key for HP.

options.text: Upper-lobe progressive massive fibrosis after coal mining
options.rationale: Upper-lobe PMF after coal mining indicates complicated CWP, not HP; a history of organic antigen exposure would be needed for HP.

options.text: Positive c-ANCA with renal involvement and hematuria
options.rationale: c-ANCA positivity with renal disease suggests GPA/Wegener, not HP; serologic vasculitis markers would redirect the diagnosis.

question: Which pulmonary finding on gross exam is most typical of advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Cobblestoned pleural surfaces from subpleural retraction
options.rationale: IPF grossly produces cobblestoned pleural surfaces due to retraction of subpleural scars, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Diffuse pleural plaques with calcification and effusion
options.rationale: Pleural plaques are associated with asbestos exposure; while plaques may coexist, cobblestoning from subpleural fibrosis is more typical of IPF.

options.text: Upper-lobe progressive massive fibrosis with cavitation
options.rationale: Upper-lobe PMF is characteristic of complicated CWP, not the lower-lobe subpleural fibrosis and cobblestoning of IPF.

options.text: Numerous small caseating granulomas with central necrosis
options.rationale: Caseating granulomas indicate TB or certain fungal infections, not the fibrotic cobblestoning of IPF; necrosis would suggest infection.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with fresh blood in airspaces
options.rationale: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage presents with blood-filled alveoli and is not the chronic fibrotic cobblestoning seen in IPF.

question: Which of the following best describes the pathologic progression seen in complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Progression from coal macules to progressive massive fibrosis
options.rationale: CWP ranges from asymptomatic anthracosis and simple coal macules to complicated disease with progressive massive fibrosis composed of dense collagen and anthracotic pigment.

options.text: Immediate development of ferruginous bodies and mesothelioma
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies and mesothelioma are asbestos-related and not the typical progression of CWP; their presence would indicate asbestos exposure.

options.text: Formation of tight noncaseating granulomas with systemic spread
options.rationale: Tight noncaseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis or berylliosis, not the fibrotic nodules and PMF of CWP; granulomas would change the diagnosis.

options.text: Acute hyaline membrane formation followed by rapid resolution
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are features of acute DAD/ARDS, not the chronic progressive fibrosis seen in complicated CWP; acute DAD would present differently.

options.text: Birefringent silica particles causing immediate necrosis
options.rationale: Birefringent silica particles are characteristic of silicosis and stimulate fibrosis, not immediate necrosis; their presence would favor silicosis over CWP.

question: Which imaging distribution differentiates asbestosis from silicosis and coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Asbestosis shows lower-lobe and subpleural predominance
options.rationale: Asbestosis preferentially localizes to lower lobes and subpleural regions near the pleura and mesothelium, distinguishing it from upper-lobe silicosis and CWP.

options.text: Silicosis shows diffuse lower-lobe honeycombing predominance
options.rationale: Silicosis typically affects upper lobes with nodules and PMF; lower-lobe honeycombing would be more typical of asbestosis or UIP.

options.text: Coal workers pneumoconiosis always spares upper lobes
options.rationale: CWP often affects upper lobes and can progress to PMF; stating it spares upper lobes contradicts the lecture and would be incorrect.

options.text: Asbestosis presents with perihilar miliary nodules
options.rationale: Perihilar miliary nodules suggest hematogenous spread or miliary infection, not the lower-lobe subpleural fibrosis of asbestosis.

options.text: Silicosis shows pleural plaques and effusions predominantly
options.rationale: Pleural plaques are characteristic of asbestos exposure, not silicosis; their presence would favor asbestosis over silicosis.

question: Which histologic description best matches the chronic lesion in ARDS when patients progress to fibrosis?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the pathogenesis and describe the morphology of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) / acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

options.text: Interstitial and intra-alveolar fibroblastic proliferation with collagen
options.rationale: The chronic/proliferative phase of DAD features interstitial and intra-alveolar fibroblastic proliferation and eventual collagen deposition leading to fibrosis.

options.text: Tight noncaseating granulomas replacing alveolar walls
options.rationale: Tight noncaseating granulomas indicate sarcoidosis, not the fibroblastic proliferation and collagen deposition of chronic DAD.

options.text: Numerous ferruginous bodies with pleural plaque formation
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies and pleural plaques are asbestos-related and not the chronic organizing lesion of ARDS; their presence would suggest asbestos exposure.

options.text: Abundant intra-alveolar macrophages with anthracotic pigment
options.rationale: Anthracotic macrophages suggest coal dust exposure; chronic DAD fibrosis is characterized by fibroblasts and collagen rather than pigment-laden macrophages.

options.text: Necrotizing vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation
options.rationale: Necrotizing vasculitis with granulomas is typical of GPA/Wegener and not the organizing fibroblastic proliferation seen in chronic DAD.

question: A patient with suspected pulmonary fibrosis asks which special stain would help assess the degree of fibrosis on biopsy. Which stain is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) / idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

options.text: Masson trichrome stain to highlight collagen deposition
options.rationale: Masson trichrome is useful to assess the degree and severity of fibrosis by highlighting collagen, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Prussian blue stain to detect fungal organisms
options.rationale: Prussian blue detects iron, not fungi; it is used for ferruginous bodies, not for assessing collagen fibrosis.

options.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain to quantify collagen fibers
options.rationale: Ziehl-Neelsen detects acid-fast bacilli and does not quantify collagen; Masson trichrome is the appropriate fibrosis stain.

options.text: Mucicarmine stain to evaluate interstitial collagen
options.rationale: Mucicarmine highlights mucin and cryptococcal capsule, not interstitial collagen; it would not assess fibrosis severity.

options.text: Periodic acid Schiff stain to measure iron deposition
options.rationale: PAS stains carbohydrates and fungal walls, not iron; Prussian blue would be used for iron detection, while Masson trichrome assesses collagen.

question: Which clinical scenario best represents the timing and symptom pattern typical of hypersensitivity pneumonitis after antigen exposure?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Symptoms begin 4 to 6 hours after exposure and recur with re-exposure
options.rationale: HP symptoms typically appear 4–6 hours after exposure and may last for hours to days, recurring with re-exposure, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Immediate anaphylactic reaction within minutes after exposure
options.rationale: Immediate IgE-mediated anaphylaxis occurs within minutes and is not the delayed 4–6 hour pattern of HP; immediate symptoms would suggest an allergic reaction.

options.text: Chronic progressive symptoms developing over decades without exposure
options.rationale: Chronic progression without ongoing exposure would be atypical for HP, which is exposure-related; chronic symptoms usually follow continued or repeated exposures.

options.text: Symptoms exclusively during sleep unrelated to exposure
options.rationale: HP is exposure-related and typically temporally linked to antigen contact; nocturnal-only symptoms without exposure history would suggest other causes.

options.text: Acute hemoptysis and renal failure at presentation
options.rationale: Acute hemoptysis and renal failure suggest vasculitis like GPA, not the typical HP presentation of fever, cough, and dyspnea after antigen exposure.

question: Which of the following best explains why asbestos exposure increases risk for bronchogenic carcinoma especially in smokers?
cited_learning_objective: Compare/contrast coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, silicosis, and asbestos-related diseases.

options.text: Asbestos fibers cause DNA damage and synergize with smoking carcinogens
options.rationale: Asbestos fibers induce fibrosis and can promote carcinogenesis; combined exposure with smoking markedly increases bronchogenic carcinoma risk, as discussed in the lecture.

options.text: Asbestos exposure primarily causes caseating granulomas leading to cancer
options.rationale: Asbestos causes fibrosis and ferruginous bodies, not caseating granulomas; caseation would suggest infection rather than asbestos-related carcinogenesis.

options.text: Asbestos exposure prevents macrophage activation reducing cancer risk
options.rationale: Asbestos does not prevent macrophage activation to reduce cancer risk; instead it contributes to chronic injury and increased malignancy risk, especially with smoking.

options.text: Asbestos fibers are inert and do not interact with tobacco smoke
options.rationale: Asbestos fibers are not inert; they interact with tobacco smoke to increase lung cancer risk, so stating no interaction contradicts lecture content.

options.text: Asbestos exposure causes immediate mesothelial necrosis that prevents tumors
options.rationale: Asbestos can cause mesothelial malignancy (mesothelioma) rather than preventing tumors; immediate necrosis preventing tumors is not supported by the lecture.

question: Which histologic feature would most likely be seen in a lung biopsy from a patient with hypersensitivity pneumonitis who has had prolonged exposure?
cited_learning_objective: Define the term hypersensitivity pneumonitis and discuss its histomorphology and associated conditions that can lead to such a reaction.

options.text: Interstitial fibrosis with fibroblastic foci and obliterative bronchiolitis
options.rationale: Chronic or continuous exposure in HP can lead to interstitial fibrosis with fibroblastic foci, honeycombing, and obliterative bronchiolitis as described in the lecture.

options.text: Acute hyaline membranes without any fibrosis
options.rationale: Hyaline membranes are acute DAD lesions; chronic prolonged HP would show fibrosis and granulomas rather than isolated hyaline membranes.

options.text: Ferruginous bodies and pleural plaques exclusively
options.rationale: Ferruginous bodies and pleural plaques indicate asbestos exposure, not chronic HP; their presence would suggest asbestosis.

options.text: Numerous caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli
options.rationale: Caseating granulomas with AFB indicate tuberculosis, not HP; positive AFB staining would change the diagnosis to mycobacterial infection.

options.text: Diffuse alveolar macrophage accumulation with anthracosis only
options.rationale: Anthracotic macrophage accumulation suggests coal dust exposure or urban pollution, not the fibrotic and granulomatous changes of chronic HP.

question: Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate before labeling a patient with noncaseating granulomas as having sarcoidosis?
cited_learning_objective: Verbally describe and visually identify sarcoidosis.

options.text: Exclude infectious and occupational causes before diagnosing sarcoidosis
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion; the lecture emphasizes ruling out TB, fungal infections, berylliosis, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis before diagnosing sarcoidosis.

options.text: Start high-dose steroids immediately without further testing
options.rationale: Immediate steroid therapy without excluding infections could be harmful; exclusion of infectious causes is necessary prior to immunosuppression.

options.text: Assume sarcoidosis if any granulomas are present regardless of context
options.rationale: Not all granulomas indicate sarcoidosis; context and exclusion of other causes are required, so assuming sarcoidosis from any granuloma is incorrect.

options.text: Treat empirically for tuberculosis in all granulomatous cases
options.rationale: Empiric TB treatment without evidence may be inappropriate; targeted testing to exclude TB is preferred before initiating therapy.

options.text: Label as hypersensitivity pneumonitis without exposure history
options.rationale: HP requires exposure to organic antigens; without exposure history, labeling as HP is unsupported and sarcoidosis remains a consideration after exclusions.
